name: Sex-positive feminism
summary: Sex-positive feminism holds that sexual freedom is essential to women's freedom and opposes legal and social controls on consensual adult sexual activity, whether they come from the state, religious conservatives or other feminists. It rejects the claim that pornography and sex work are inherently degrading, supports decriminalising sex work, and defends sexual minorities, treating consent as the central test. It emerged from the 1980s feminist sex wars as a response to the anti-pornography feminism of Andrea Dworkin and Catharine MacKinnon.
scope: The pro-sex (sex-radical) strand of US-centred feminism that formed in the feminist sex wars from the late 1970s: Ellen Willis, who coined "pro-sex feminism"; Gayle Rubin (Thinking Sex, 1984) and Carole Vance with the 1982 Barnard conference and Pleasure and Danger; the Feminist Anti-Censorship Task Force; Pat Califia and Samois; and later writers such as Carol Queen and Nadine Strossen. Defining sources (Stanford Encyclopedia, OutHistory, The Conversation, the New York Times, the Guardian) treat it as sexual freedom being essential to women's freedom, opposition to censorship of sexual expression, defence of sexual minorities, and critique of anti-pornography feminism. It does not cover feminism generally or non-feminist sexual-liberation movements. Because it is a movement about sexuality, most economic, foreign-policy and constitutional questions are unaddressed.
